objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: Your retrieval service reads from Cosmos DB for NoSQL at Strong consistency. Read charges are twice what you budgeted. Users only ever read their own writes, from a single region. Which change reduces RU cost with no correctness impact for that pattern?

options.text: Switch the default consistency level to Session
Switch to Bounded Staleness with a small lag window
Enable autoscale throughput
Add a composite index covering the query

explanation: Reads at Strong and Bounded Staleness are charged at double the RU rate of Session, Consistent Prefix and Eventual. Session guarantees read-your-own-writes within a session, which is precisely the stated requirement, so it halves read cost without breaking anything.

whyWrong.B: Bounded Staleness is in the same 2× RU band as Strong, so it saves nothing.
whyWrong.C: Autoscale changes how throughput is provisioned and billed, not the RU cost of each read — and it costs 1.5× per RU.
whyWrong.D: Composite indexes help multi-property ORDER BY. They do not change the consistency multiplier on reads.

docs.title: Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: What is the default consistency level for a new Azure Cosmos DB account?

options.text: Session
Strong
Eventual
Consistent Prefix

explanation: Session is the default. It is the middle of the five levels and gives read-your-own-writes and monotonic reads within a session, at the cheaper read rate.

whyWrong.B: Strong is the strictest level and must be chosen deliberately; it also doubles read RU charges.
whyWrong.C: Eventual is the weakest level and is not the default.
whyWrong.D: Consistent Prefix guarantees ordering without recency and is not the default.

docs.title: Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: A managed identity has been granted the Cosmos DB Account Reader Role on the account. The application authenticates successfully but every document read returns 403 Forbidden. What is missing?

options.text: A data-plane role assignment, created with `az cosmosdb sql role assignment create`
The Contributor role on the resource group
A firewall rule allowing the application's outbound IP
Enabling the local authentication keys on the account

explanation: Cosmos DB separates control plane from data plane. Azure RBAC roles such as Account Reader or even Owner govern the resource, not the documents. Reading items requires a Cosmos DB data-plane role assignment created with `az cosmosdb sql role assignment create`.

whyWrong.B: Contributor is another control-plane role and grants no data access at all.
whyWrong.C: A firewall block produces a network-level failure, not a 403 after successful authentication.
whyWrong.D: The scenario uses a managed identity, so key-based auth is irrelevant — and enabling keys weakens security.

docs.title: Data plane RBAC in Cosmos DB

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: You are adding vector search to a Cosmos DB for NoSQL container holding several million chunks. Which vector index type is designed for large datasets with low query latency?

options.text: `diskANN`
flat
`quantizedFlat`
composite

explanation: Cosmos DB offers flat (exact search, small sets), `quantizedFlat` (compressed vectors, medium sets) and `diskANN` (a graph index built for large-scale approximate search with low latency). Several million vectors is `diskANN` territory.

whyWrong.B: flat performs an exact scan and does not scale to millions of vectors.
whyWrong.C: quantizedFlat improves on flat by compressing vectors but is still not the large-scale option.
whyWrong.D: composite is a regular index type for multi-property ORDER BY, not a vector index.

docs.title: Vector search in Cosmos DB for NoSQL

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: A change feed processor keeps documents in a search index up to date. Deleted documents remain in the index indefinitely. What explains this?

options.text: The default latest-version change feed mode does not emit delete events
The lease container is missing, so checkpoints are lost
The processor is running with too few instances to keep up
Deletes are only emitted at the Strong consistency level

explanation: In latest-version mode the change feed reports inserts and updates only. Deletes are invisible. The two standard remedies are all-versions-and-deletes mode, or soft-delete: mark the item deleted and set a TTL so the update flows through the feed.

whyWrong.B: A missing lease container breaks checkpointing entirely — you would see reprocessing, not selectively missing deletes.
whyWrong.C: Insufficient instances causes lag across all change types, not the permanent absence of one type.
whyWrong.D: Change feed behaviour is not governed by the account consistency level.

docs.title: Change feed in Azure Cosmos DB

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: You are implementing a change feed processor in the .NET SDK. Which component is required in addition to the monitored container?

options.text: A lease container that stores checkpoints and distributes partitions across instances
An Event Hubs namespace to buffer changes
A second Cosmos DB account in a paired region
A stored procedure registered on the monitored container

explanation: The change feed processor stores its position in a lease container. Leases are also how work is divided between instances, so running more instances against the same lease container is how you scale out.

whyWrong.B: Event Hubs is not part of the change feed processor; the feed is read directly from the container.
whyWrong.C: A second account relates to geo-replication, not the change feed.
whyWrong.D: Stored procedures execute inside a partition on demand and have no role in change feed processing.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: Write throughput charges on a container are much higher than expected. Documents contain a large embedding array and several long text fields that are never used in filters. What is the most effective change?

options.text: Add the unused paths to excludedPaths in the container's indexing policy
Switch the indexing mode from consistent to none
Lower the account consistency level to Eventual
Enable autoscale throughput on the container

explanation: Cosmos DB indexes every path by default, and each indexed path adds RU cost to every write. Excluding paths you never filter or sort on is the standard way to cut write charges while keeping queries working.

whyWrong.B: Indexing mode none disables indexing altogether, so all queries degrade to full scans — far too blunt.
whyWrong.C: Consistency affects read costs, not write indexing costs.
whyWrong.D: Autoscale changes billing shape, not the RU consumed per write.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: A query with ORDER BY c.tenantId, c.createdAt fails with an error stating that the query requires an index that is not configured. What do you add?

options.text: A composite index on tenantId and createdAt in the indexing policy
A spatial index on both properties
A unique key policy on tenantId and createdAt
A vector index covering both properties

explanation: Range indexes cover single-property ORDER BY. Sorting on two or more properties requires a composite index that lists them in the same order and direction as the query.

whyWrong.B: Spatial indexes serve geospatial types and operators.
whyWrong.C: A unique key policy enforces uniqueness within a partition; it does not enable sorting.
whyWrong.D: Vector indexes serve VectorDistance similarity search only.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: Your service returns HTTP 429 from Cosmos DB during traffic spikes, always on documents belonging to the same large customer. Throughput is already provisioned generously. What is the underlying problem?

options.text: A hot logical partition — the partition key concentrates that customer's traffic on one partition
The SDK is configured in gateway mode instead of direct mode
The account is at Session consistency instead of Strong
Autoscale is disabled on the container

explanation: Provisioned throughput is divided evenly across physical partitions. A partition key that funnels one tenant's traffic into a single logical partition means that partition can only ever use its share, so it throttles while the rest of the container sits idle.

whyWrong.B: Gateway mode adds latency but does not cause partition-level throttling.
whyWrong.C: Consistency affects RU per read, not the distribution of load across partitions.
whyWrong.D: Autoscale would raise the ceiling, but the per-partition share is still a fraction of the total — the skew remains.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: How should `CosmosClient` be managed in an ASP.NET Core application?

options.text: Registered as a singleton and reused for the lifetime of the application
Created per request in a using block and disposed
Registered as scoped so each request gets its own instance
Created per container to isolate connection pools

explanation: `CosmosClient` is thread-safe and maintains connections and routing caches internally. Creating one per request wastes connections and adds cold-start latency to every call, so a singleton is the documented pattern.

whyWrong.B: Disposing per request tears down the connection pool constantly and is a known performance anti-pattern.
whyWrong.C: Scoped is per request, with the same problem.
whyWrong.D: One client can address any number of databases and containers; extra clients gain nothing.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: Which property of the SDK response tells you the RU cost of an operation you just performed?

options.text: response.`RequestCharge`
response.Diagnostics.Duration
response.ActivityId
response.ETag

explanation: `RequestCharge` surfaces the x-ms-request-charge header and reports the RUs consumed. Logging it per operation is how you find the queries that are actually costing you throughput.

whyWrong.B: Duration measures elapsed time, which is related but not the billing unit.
whyWrong.C: ActivityId correlates a request with server-side traces for support.
whyWrong.D: ETag supports optimistic concurrency.

docs.title: Request units in Azure Cosmos DB

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: A nightly job writes two million embedding documents. It runs slowly and generates constant 429s despite generous throughput. Which SDK setting is designed for this workload?

options.text: Set `AllowBulkExecution` to true on the `CosmosClient`Options
Set ConnectionMode to Gateway
Set ConsistencyLevel to Eventual on each write
Set `EnableContentResponseOnWrite` to true

explanation: Bulk mode batches concurrent operations by physical partition and manages the rate for you, which is exactly what a high-volume ingest needs. It trades per-operation latency for throughput.

whyWrong.B: Gateway mode adds a hop and generally reduces throughput compared with direct mode.
whyWrong.C: Consistency does not change write throughput limits.
whyWrong.D: Returning the written document on every write increases payload size — for bulk ingest you normally set this to false.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: A query filters on a single tenant's documents, and tenantId is the partition key. Query costs are far higher than expected. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The partition key is not being passed in `QueryRequestOptions`, so the query fans out across all partitions
The container is using autoscale throughput
The query is missing a TOP clause
The account is configured for multi-region writes

explanation: Even when the filter names the partition key property, supplying `PartitionKey` in `QueryRequestOptions` is what routes the query to a single physical partition. Without it the SDK may fan out, multiplying the RU charge.

whyWrong.B: Autoscale affects provisioning and billing rate, not the RU cost of a given query.
whyWrong.C: TOP limits rows returned but does not reduce the partitions scanned.
whyWrong.D: Multi-region writes affect write routing and conflict handling, not single-partition query cost.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: Which elements must be declared in a container's vector embedding policy before you can run vector search? Choose three.

options.text: The JSON path of the embedding property
The number of dimensions
The distance function
The embedding model deployment name
The partition key of the container

explanation: The vector embedding policy declares path, data type, dimensions and distance function (cosine, dotproduct or euclidean). A matching vector index is then added to the indexing policy.

whyWrong.D: Cosmos DB stores vectors; it does not generate them, so it never needs to know which model produced them.
whyWrong.E: The partition key is part of the container definition, not the vector policy.

docs.title: Vector search in Cosmos DB for NoSQL

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: Chat sessions must be removed automatically 30 days after their last update, without a cleanup job. What do you configure?

options.text: Time to live on the container, with the value expressed in seconds
A change feed processor that deletes old items
A retention policy on the Cosmos DB account
An analytical store with a 30-day retention window

explanation: Container-level TTL expires items automatically, in seconds, using leftover throughput. Items can override it with their own ttl property. This is the intended answer whenever a scenario says 'without writing a cleanup job'.

whyWrong.B: This is the cleanup job the requirement rules out, and it consumes RUs you would otherwise not spend.
whyWrong.C: There is no account-level document retention policy.
whyWrong.D: The analytical store is for analytics workloads and does not delete data from the transactional store.

docs.title: Time to live in Azure Cosmos DB

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: You run `CREATE EXTENSION vector`; on Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server and it fails with an error saying the extension is not allow-listed. What must you do first?

options.text: Add vector to the `azure.extensions` server parameter and let the change apply
Restart the server so the extension binaries are loaded
Grant the connecting user the azure_pg_admin role
Upgrade the server to a memory-optimized SKU

explanation: Flexible server keeps an allowlist of permitted extensions in the `azure.extensions` server parameter. The extension must be added there before CREATE EXTENSION will succeed in any database.

whyWrong.B: A restart alone changes nothing while the extension remains off the allowlist.
whyWrong.C: Role membership governs who may create extensions, but the allowlist is checked regardless of role.
whyWrong.D: SKU affects performance for vector workloads; it has no bearing on whether the extension may be created.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: Your embeddings are normalised and you want cosine similarity. Which operator do you use in the ORDER BY clause?
explanation: `pgvector` uses <=> for cosine distance, <-> for L2/Euclidean and <#> for negative inner product. The index's operator class must match the operator you query with, or the planner will fall back to a sequential scan.

whyWrong.B: <-> is Euclidean distance.
whyWrong.C: <#> is negative inner product — negated so that smaller means more similar.
whyWrong.D: @> is the containment operator for arrays and JSON, unrelated to vectors.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: You create an IVFFlat index on an empty embeddings table, then load two million rows. Recall is poor and results look arbitrary. What went wrong?

options.text: IVFFlat centroids are computed from the data present when the index is built
IVFFlat does not support the cosine operator class for normalised vectors
The lists parameter must be set to the number of rows in the table
IVFFlat requires vectors to be normalised to unit length before insert

explanation: IVFFlat partitions the vector space using centroids computed at build time. Build it on an empty table and the partitioning does not reflect your data, so probes land in the wrong lists. Rebuild the index after loading, or use HNSW, which can be built incrementally.

whyWrong.B: IVFFlat supports vector_cosine_ops as well as L2 and inner product.
whyWrong.C: lists is a tuning parameter, typically rows/1000 up to a million rows and around the square root above that — never the row count.
whyWrong.D: Normalisation matters for choosing a metric, not for whether IVFFlat functions.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: Which statements about HNSW indexes in `pgvector` are correct? Choose two.

options.text: They can be created on an empty table and stay effective as rows are inserted
They generally give better recall and query latency than IVFFlat at the same dataset size
They use less memory than IVFFlat
They are built faster than IVFFlat
They guarantee exact nearest-neighbour results

explanation: HNSW builds a navigable graph incrementally, so it works on an empty table and generally beats IVFFlat on recall and latency. The trade-offs are higher memory use and slower index builds.

whyWrong.C: HNSW uses more memory, which is its main cost.
whyWrong.D: HNSW builds are slower; that is the other half of the trade-off.
whyWrong.E: Both HNSW and IVFFlat are approximate. Only an exact scan guarantees true nearest neighbours.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: Recall from your HNSW-indexed similarity search is too low for production. Which query-time setting raises recall at the cost of latency?

options.text: `SET hnsw.ef_search = 200;`
`SET ivfflat.probes = 200;`
`SET work_mem = '256MB';`
`SET enable_seqscan = off;`

explanation: `hnsw.ef_search` controls how many candidates the graph traversal keeps in its dynamic list. Raising it explores more of the graph, improving recall and increasing query time. The IVFFlat equivalent is `ivfflat.probes`.

whyWrong.B: probes applies to IVFFlat indexes and has no effect on an HNSW index.
whyWrong.C: work_mem sizes sorts and hashes; it does not change ANN search breadth.
whyWrong.D: Disabling sequential scans nudges the planner toward indexes but does not affect recall within the index.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: A multi-tenant RAG query filters on tenant_id and orders by vector distance. For small tenants it frequently returns fewer than the requested ten rows, even though the tenant has hundreds of chunks. Why?
code:
SELECT id, content
FROM chunks
WHERE tenant_id = $1
ORDER BY embedding <=> $2
LIMIT 10;

options.text: The ANN index returns a bounded candidate set before the filter is applied
The vector column contains NULLs for that tenant's newer chunks
LIMIT cannot be combined with a vector ORDER BY in the same query
The tenant_id column lacks an index, so the filter is not pushed down

explanation: The approximate index is searched first and yields a bounded candidate list; the WHERE filter is then applied to those candidates. For a selective filter most candidates are discarded. The fixes are partial indexes per tenant, iterative scans, or raising `ef_search`/probes so the candidate pool is larger.

whyWrong.B: NULL embeddings would be a data problem affecting all tenants equally, not a size-dependent shortfall.
whyWrong.C: LIMIT with a vector ORDER BY is the standard KNN query form.
whyWrong.D: A nullability constraint has no bearing on how many rows a filtered ANN query returns.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: An Azure Function scales out to hundreds of concurrent instances, each opening a PostgreSQL connection. The database starts rejecting connections. What is the recommended fix on flexible server?

options.text: Route connections through the built-in `PgBouncer` on port 6432 in transaction pooling mode
Raise max_connections to several thousand
Move the database to a read replica
Switch the client library to use SSL

explanation: Flexible server includes `PgBouncer`, exposed on port 6432. Transaction pooling multiplexes many short-lived client connections onto a small pool of server connections, which is exactly the serverless fan-out pattern.

whyWrong.B: Each Postgres connection is a backend process consuming memory; raising the limit trades connection errors for memory pressure and instability.
whyWrong.C: Read replicas add read capacity but do nothing about connection count on writes.
whyWrong.D: TLS is about transport security and is unrelated to connection exhaustion.

docs.title: PgBouncer in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: You need to confirm that a similarity query is actually using the vector index rather than scanning the table. What do you run?

options.text: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on the query and check for an `Index Scan` rather than a `Seq Scan`
`SELECT * FROM pg_indexes` to confirm the index exists
VACUUM ANALYZE on the table
`SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('idx_embedding'))`

explanation: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows the plan the planner actually chose plus real timings. A `Seq Scan` on a table with a vector index usually means an operator/operator-class mismatch or statistics that make the scan look cheaper.

whyWrong.B: That confirms the index exists, not that the planner chose it — the common failure is an index that exists and is ignored.
whyWrong.C: VACUUM ANALYZE refreshes statistics and may change the plan, but it does not show you the plan.
whyWrong.D: Index size tells you nothing about plan selection.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: Which column definition stores embeddings from a model that produces 1536-dimensional vectors?

options.text: embedding vector(1536)
embedding float8[1536]
embedding numeric(1536)
embedding jsonb

explanation: `pgvector` introduces the vector type with a fixed dimension, which is required for indexing and for the distance operators to work.

whyWrong.B: A float array stores the numbers but supports none of the vector operators or indexes.
whyWrong.C: numeric(1536) declares precision on a single number, not a 1536-element vector.
whyWrong.D: jsonb can hold the array as data but cannot be indexed for similarity search.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: Building an HNSW index over ten million embeddings takes many hours. Which server-side change most directly speeds up the build?

options.text: Raise `maintenance_work_mem` so the build stays in memory, and increase max_parallel_maintenance_workers
Raise shared_buffers to 90% of available RAM
Lower `hnsw.ef_search` before creating the index
Disable autovacuum for the duration of the build

explanation: Index builds are bounded by `maintenance_work_mem` — once the build spills to disk it slows dramatically. Parallel maintenance workers then divide the work across cores.

whyWrong.B: shared_buffers is the general page cache and is not what an index build allocates from; over-sizing it starves everything else.
whyWrong.C: ef_search is a query-time parameter. The build-time equivalents are m and ef_construction.
whyWrong.D: Autovacuum is not the bottleneck, and disabling it invites bloat.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: Vector queries on a 20 GB index are slow and the server shows heavy disk read activity. CPU sits at 30%. Which compute change helps most?

options.text: Move to a memory-optimized SKU with enough RAM to hold the index
Move to a compute-optimized SKU with more vCPUs
Increase the storage size to raise the IOPS allocation
Enable high availability with a standby replica

explanation: Low CPU with heavy disk reads means the working set does not fit in memory. Vector indexes are traversed randomly, so paging from disk dominates. Memory-optimized SKUs give the highest RAM per vCPU.

whyWrong.B: More cores do not help when the bottleneck is I/O, as the 30% CPU figure shows.
whyWrong.C: More IOPS softens the symptom but keeps every traversal on disk; keeping the index in memory removes the reads.
whyWrong.D: HA provides failover, not query performance.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: Index memory for your vector column must be reduced with only a small loss of recall. Which `pgvector` feature addresses this directly?

options.text: Store the column as `halfvec`, using 16-bit floats
Reduce the vector dimension by truncating the arrays in the application
Switch the index operator class to `vector_l2_ops`
Enable table compression on the embeddings table

explanation: `halfvec` stores each component as a 16-bit float, roughly halving index memory for a small recall cost. It is the built-in answer to memory pressure on vector indexes.

whyWrong.B: Arbitrary truncation destroys the geometry of the embedding space unless the model explicitly supports shortened dimensions.
whyWrong.C: The operator class must match your distance metric; changing it changes semantics, not memory.
whyWrong.D: There is no table compression setting in PostgreSQL that shrinks an index this way.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: A RAG pipeline must retrieve chunks for one document only, and that filter is highly selective. Which indexing strategy gives the most reliable results?

options.text: A partial vector index defined WHERE the filter matches, or a composite strategy that keeps filtered candidates in the index
A B-tree index on document_id alone
A single HNSW index over all embeddings with no filter-aware strategy
A GIN index on the embedding column

explanation: Highly selective filters combined with ANN search are the classic under-retrieval case. A partial index restricted to the filtered subset means the ANN traversal only ever visits relevant rows.

whyWrong.B: A B-tree on document_id speeds the filter but the vector ordering still needs a vector index.
whyWrong.C: This is precisely the configuration that under-returns when the filter is selective.
whyWrong.D: GIN indexes serve arrays, full-text and JSON — not vector distance.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: Which approach lets an application connect to Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server without storing a password?

options.text: Microsoft Entra ID authentication, using an access token from the app's managed identity as the password
Storing the password in Key Vault and reading it at startup
Using a connection string with TrustServerCertificate=true
Enabling public network access with a firewall rule for the app's IP

explanation: Flexible server supports Entra ID authentication: the client acquires a token for the managed identity and presents it in place of a password. No secret is stored anywhere.

whyWrong.B: This is better than hard-coding, but a password still exists and must be rotated — the requirement was no stored password.
whyWrong.C: That setting relaxes certificate validation and has nothing to do with credentials.
whyWrong.D: Firewall rules control who may connect, not how they authenticate.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: You want to generate embeddings for new rows by calling Azure OpenAI directly from SQL, without an application tier. Which Azure extension provides this?

options.text: `azure_ai`
pg_cron
postgres_fdw
`pg_diskann`

explanation: The `azure_ai` extension exposes functions that call Azure OpenAI and other Azure AI services from within SQL, so an INSERT can produce its own embedding. Like any extension it must be allow-listed in `azure.extensions` first.

whyWrong.B: pg_cron schedules SQL jobs inside the database but cannot call an external service by itself.
whyWrong.C: postgres_fdw connects to other PostgreSQL servers.
whyWrong.D: pg_diskann provides a vector index type, not model invocation.

objective: Integrate Azure Managed Redis in AI solutions
stem: You cache LLM responses in Azure Managed Redis. Cached answers must expire after 15 minutes. Which command sets the value and its expiry in a single round trip?

options.text: `SET response:abc123 "..." EX 900`
`SET response:abc123 "..." then EXPIRE response:abc123 900`
`SETNX` response:abc123 "..." EX 900
`HSET` response:abc123 ttl 900

explanation: SET with the EX option writes the value and the TTL atomically in one round trip. The two-command form leaves a window in which the key exists with no expiry, and it costs an extra round trip.

whyWrong.B: Two commands means two round trips and a window where a crash leaves the key immortal.
whyWrong.C: SETNX only writes when the key does not exist, which is not what a cache refresh needs.
whyWrong.D: HSET writes a hash field. Storing 900 in a field called ttl does not make Redis expire anything.

objective: Integrate Azure Managed Redis in AI solutions
stem: A product catalogue is cached in Redis and read heavily. When a product is updated in the source database, the cache must not serve stale data. Which approach is most robust?

options.text: Delete the cache key on update and let the next read repopulate it
Write the new value to the cache immediately after updating the database
Reduce the TTL to one second for all product keys
Call `FLUSHALL` after every write to the database

explanation: Invalidate-on-write is the standard cache-aside pattern. Deleting is safer than updating: if the database write succeeds and the cache write fails, a deleted key simply causes a miss, whereas a failed update can leave a stale value behind indefinitely.

whyWrong.B: Write-through is workable but has a race: two concurrent updates can write their values to the cache in the opposite order to the database.
whyWrong.C: A one-second TTL destroys the hit rate and still allows a second of staleness.
whyWrong.D: FLUSHALL wipes the entire cache and would cause a thundering herd on every write.

objective: Integrate Azure Managed Redis in AI solutions
stem: Cached items disappear well before their TTL expires and the cache reports high memory usage. Which configuration change addresses the cause?

options.text: Move to a larger tier or set an eviction policy appropriate to the workload, since Redis is evicting under memory pressure
Lower the TTL so keys expire more predictably
Switch the clustering policy from OSS to Enterprise
Enable AOF persistence

explanation: Keys vanishing early with memory pressure is eviction, not expiry. Either give the cache more memory or choose a policy that matches the workload — `allkeys-lru` for a pure cache, `volatile-lru` when only some keys are disposable.

whyWrong.B: Shorter TTLs reduce the hit rate without fixing the underlying shortage.
whyWrong.C: Clustering policy affects key distribution and client behaviour, not memory capacity.
whyWrong.D: Persistence protects against data loss on restart and actually adds overhead.

objective: Integrate Azure Managed Redis in AI solutions
stem: You want to use Azure Managed Redis as a vector store for semantic caching. Which command creates the index?

options.text: `FT.CREATE idx ON HASH PREFIX 1 doc: SCHEMA embedding VECTOR HNSW 6 TYPE FLOAT32 DIM 1536 DISTANCE_METRIC COSINE`
VADD idx embedding 1536 COSINE
`ZADD` idx 1536 embedding
`CREATE INDEX idx ON doc (embedding) USING hnsw`

explanation: Vector search in Redis comes from the RediSearch module. `FT.CREATE` defines the index, and a VECTOR field declares the algorithm (HNSW or FLAT), element type, dimension and distance metric.

whyWrong.B: Not a Redis command.
whyWrong.C: ZADD adds to a sorted set — one score per member, not a vector index.
whyWrong.D: That is SQL syntax, not Redis.

docs.title: Vector search in Azure Managed Redis

objective: Integrate Azure Managed Redis in AI solutions
stem: Which query returns the five nearest neighbours to a supplied vector from a RediSearch vector index?

options.text: `FT.SEARCH idx "*=>[KNN 5 @embedding $vec AS score]" PARAMS 2 vec <bytes> DIALECT 2`
`FT.SEARCH idx "@embedding:[0 5]"`
`GEORADIUS idx 0 0 5 km WITHDIST COUNT 5`
`ZRANGEBYSCORE idx 0 5 WITHSCORES LIMIT 0 5`

explanation: KNN queries use the *=>[KNN k @field $param AS alias] syntax, with the query vector supplied through PARAMS as raw bytes and DIALECT 2 or higher enabled.

whyWrong.B: That is numeric range syntax for a scalar field.
whyWrong.C: GEORADIUS performs geospatial search on latitude/longitude.
whyWrong.D: ZRANGEBYSCORE reads a sorted set by score.

objective: Integrate Azure Managed Redis in AI solutions
stem: A troubleshooting script runs KEYS session:* against a production Redis instance with millions of keys. What is the consequence, and what should be used instead?

options.text: KEYS blocks the server for the duration of the scan; use `SCAN`, which iterates in small batches with a cursor
KEYS returns at most 1000 keys; use KEYS with a higher COUNT
KEYS is fine but returns keys in random order; use SORT to stabilise it
KEYS only matches exact names; use MATCH instead

explanation: Redis executes commands on a single thread, so KEYS blocks every other client until it has walked the entire keyspace. `SCAN` returns a cursor and small batches, letting other commands interleave.

whyWrong.B: KEYS has no COUNT option and no result cap — it returns everything that matches, which is the problem.
whyWrong.C: Ordering is not the issue; server blocking is.
whyWrong.D: KEYS does support glob patterns, and MATCH is an option of SCAN, not a command.

objective: Integrate Azure Managed Redis in AI solutions
stem: An ASP.NET Core service shows intermittent Redis timeouts under load. Investigation shows a new `ConnectionMultiplexer` is created for each request. What is the fix?

options.text: Create one `ConnectionMultiplexer` and share it as a singleton for the application's lifetime
Increase the connect timeout in the connection string
Create one multiplexer per Redis database index
Disable connection pooling in the client library

explanation: `ConnectionMultiplexer` is designed to be shared: it is thread-safe and multiplexes all commands over a small number of connections. Creating one per request exhausts sockets and produces exactly this timeout pattern.

whyWrong.B: A longer timeout hides the symptom while connection churn continues.
whyWrong.C: One multiplexer can address any database via GetDatabase(n).
whyWrong.D: Multiplexing is the mechanism that makes the client efficient; disabling it makes things worse.

objective: Integrate Azure Managed Redis in AI solutions
stem: Which Azure Managed Redis tier is the best starting point for a workload dominated by vector similarity search across a large index?

options.text: Compute Optimized, which provides the highest vCPU-to-memory ratio for search-heavy workloads
Flash Optimized, which stores data on NVMe
Memory Optimized, which maximises memory per vCPU
Any tier — vector search performance does not vary by tier

explanation: Vector search is computationally intensive per query, so it benefits from more processing power per unit of memory. Compute Optimized is the tier Microsoft recommends for search-heavy workloads, including vector search.

whyWrong.B: Flash Optimized trades speed for capacity on colder data — the opposite of what latency-sensitive search needs.
whyWrong.C: Memory Optimized suits large datasets with light compute, such as a plain cache.
whyWrong.D: Tier selection materially changes vector search throughput and latency.

stem: You are implementing a semantic cache in front of an expensive LLM call. Which sequence describes the correct lookup?

options.text: Embed the prompt, run a KNN query against the cache index, and return the cached answer only if the nearest match is within a similarity threshold
Hash the prompt text and look up the hash with GET
Run a KNN query and always return the nearest match
Store every prompt in a sorted set and use ZRANGEBYLEX for prefix matching

explanation: Semantic caching matches on meaning rather than exact text, so it embeds the incoming prompt and does a nearest-neighbour lookup. The similarity threshold is essential — without it the cache confidently returns answers to different questions.

whyWrong.B: Exact hashing is a plain cache and misses any paraphrase, which is the whole point of semantic caching.
whyWrong.C: There is always a nearest match. Without a threshold you serve wrong answers.
whyWrong.D: Lexical prefix matching does not capture semantic similarity.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: Traffic to your Cosmos DB container is spiky: near zero for hours, then short bursts ten times the baseline. Which throughput model is most cost-effective?

options.text: Autoscale, which scales between 10% and 100% of the maximum RU/s you set
Manual throughput provisioned at the peak rate
Manual throughput provisioned at the average rate
Serverless, regardless of the account's other workloads

explanation: Autoscale is built for unpredictable, spiky traffic: you set a maximum and are billed for the highest RU/s used each hour, down to 10% of the maximum. The 1.5× per-RU premium is easily beaten by not paying peak rates all day.

whyWrong.B: Provisioning for peak means paying for peak during the many idle hours.
whyWrong.C: Provisioning at the average guarantees throttling during every burst.
whyWrong.D: Serverless suits low-volume, intermittent workloads but has lower throughput ceilings; a ten-times burst may exceed them.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
stem: Your service handles occasional 429 responses from Cosmos DB. What is the recommended client behaviour?

options.text: Let the SDK retry automatically, and tune MaxRetryAttemptsOnRateLimitedRequests and MaxRetryWaitTimeOnRateLimitedRequests if needed
Catch the exception and retry immediately in a tight loop
Fail the request and surface a 503 to the caller
Switch the client to gateway mode, which does not return 429

explanation: The SDK already honours the retry-after hint the service returns and retries transparently. The options let you widen or narrow that window; hand-rolled retry logic usually ignores retry-after and makes throttling worse.

whyWrong.B: Immediate retries ignore retry-after and amplify the overload.
whyWrong.C: 429 is a transient, retryable condition — failing the request wastes a request that would have succeeded.
whyWrong.D: Connection mode does not change throughput enforcement; both modes see 429.
